q: Under which arrangement does the investment banker guarantee the issuer the full proceeds and absorb the loss on any shares it cannot sell?
o: Firm commitment underwriting
Best efforts underwriting
Private placement
Green shoe option
e: In a firm commitment the underwriter buys the entire issue at a set price and resells it, so any shares left unsold are its loss. Under best efforts the banker only tries to sell as much as possible and the company bears the shortfall.

q: Which of these fictional clients qualifies as an accredited investor under Rule 501 of Regulation D?
o: Ivan, net worth of $1.5 million, of which $700,000 is equity in his primary residence
Rosa and Tom, joint income of $320,000 in each of the last two years, expecting the same this year
Leah, single, income of $185,000 in each of the last two years and expecting a raise
A local charity whose total assets are $4 million
e: Natural persons qualify with joint income above $300,000 (or above $200,000 alone) in each of the two most recent years plus a reasonable expectation of the same (2026 edition figure), or net worth above $1 million excluding the primary residence. Charities need assets above $5 million.

q: A dealer quotes Harbor Corp. at $18.40 bid and $18.55 ask. A client sells 200 shares to the dealer. Which statement is correct?
o: The client receives $18.55 a share, since a dealer buys at its ask
The dealer is acting as the client's agent and earns a commission
The client receives $18.40 a share, since a dealer buys at its bid
The dealer is called a specialist because the trade is over the counter
e: A dealer is a principal who quotes a two-sided market: it buys at the bid and sells at the higher ask. On an exchange the dealer is a specialist; in the OTC market it is a market maker. A broker, by contrast, is an agent paid a commission.

q:
Which statements about venture capital are correct?
I. It typically finances privately held companies, often through convertible preferred stock.
II. It tends to have a low correlation with equities.
III. VC firms usually stay passive and avoid advising company management.
IV. Bridge financing is capital provided ahead of an expected IPO.
o: I and III only
II and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
I, II, and IV
e: Venture capital funds private companies (often with convertible preferred), is high risk/high return, illiquid, and has low correlation with equities. VC firms usually advise management and aim to exit in roughly 5–10 years, ideally by IPO. Bridge financing supports an expected IPO.

q: Marcus, 58, has moderate risk tolerance, wants diversification and professional management, and may need his money within a few years. A friend pitches an oil-and-gas limited partnership. What is the best advice?
o: Buy the LP, since limited partners decide when distributions are paid
Buy the LP, since partnership income is passed through to him tax-free
Favor a mutual fund or ETF; the LP is likely illiquid and its resale may be restricted
Join as the general partner, which limits his personal liability
e: LP interests are generally riskier than bonds or listed stocks, usually illiquid, give limited partners no management role, and may be hard to sell. Mutual funds or ETFs offer diversification and professional management with less marketability and liquidity risk, so LPs are generally unsuitable for the average investor.

q: Northgate Robotics sells new shares in its IPO at $20 each, paying underwriting costs of $1.40 a share. A week later, Kai buys 1,000 Northgate shares on the exchange at $26. How much of Kai's money goes to Northgate?
e: Only primary-market sales send money (less underwriting costs) to the issuer. Kai's purchase is a secondary-market trade between investors, so Northgate receives nothing: 1,000 × $26 = $26,000 goes to the selling investor.

q: Bianca sells short 300 shares of Lumen Co. at $60 with a 50% initial margin. Lumen pays a $0.80 per-share dividend before she covers, and she buys the shares back at $52. What is her percentage return?
e: Deposit = 300 × $60 × 0.50 = $9,000. Proceeds $18,000 − cost to cover $15,600 = $2,400 gain. Less dividend paid 300 × $0.80 = $240 → net profit $2,160. Return = $2,160 ÷ $9,000 = 24.00%.

q: Elena buys 500 shares at $48 in her margin account with a 50% initial margin. Her broker's maintenance margin is 30%. At about what share price will she receive a margin call?
e: Margin-call price = [purchase price × (1 − initial margin)] ÷ (1 − maintenance margin) = ($48 × 0.50) ÷ (1 − 0.30) = $24 ÷ 0.70 = $34.29.

q: Elena bought 500 shares at $48 on 50% initial margin, so she owes the broker $24 a share. The stock drops to $30 and the maintenance margin is 30%. How much cash must she deposit to restore the required equity?
e: Required equity = $30 × 0.30 = $9.00 a share. Actual equity = $30 − $24 loan = $6.00. Shortfall = $3.00 × 500 shares = $1,500.

q: Arjun buys 200 shares at $50 using 50% margin at 7% annual interest. During the year the stock pays a $1 per-share dividend, and he sells all shares at $58 at year-end. What is his holding period return?
e: Ending $11,600 − beginning $10,000 + dividends $200 − interest (7% × $5,000 loan) $350 = $1,450. His investment = 50% × $10,000 = $5,000. HPR = $1,450 ÷ $5,000 = 29%.

q: Noor owns 800 shares trading at $70. She wants out if the stock falls to $62, but will not accept any sale below $62, even if that means she may not get out. Which order fits?
o: Sell stop at $62
Sell stop-limit at $62
Buy stop at $62
Sell limit at $62
e: A stop-limit triggers at the stop price and then becomes a limit order, so it never fills below the limit. The trade-off: if the stock gaps through $62 and keeps falling, it may never execute. A plain stop becomes a market order and guarantees execution, not price.

q: Theo sold short 500 shares at $35 and wants to cap his loss if the stock rallies. Which order should he enter?
o: Sell stop at $30
Buy limit at $30
Buy stop at $40
Sell stop at $40
e: A short seller loses when the price rises, so protection is a buy stop placed above the current price. If the stock trades at or through $40, the order becomes a market order to buy and cover the 500 shares.

q: A brokerage firm holding a client's securities in street name goes bankrupt. Which statement about SIPC is correct?
o: It covers up to $250,000 per customer, all of which may be securities
It covers up to $500,000 per customer, including up to $250,000 of cash
It covers market losses incurred while waiting for securities to be returned
It covers only certificates held by the client, not street-name holdings
e: SIPC oversees the liquidation of failed brokerage firms and covers each customer up to $500,000, of which no more than $250,000 may be cash (2026 edition figure). It does not protect against market losses.

q: Celia asks which of her holdings can be cashed in quickly at a known value but has no market where she could sell it to another investor. Which holding fits?
o: Her 26-week Treasury bill
Her negotiable CD
Her bank money market deposit account
Shares of a privately held company
e: Liquidity means converting to cash quickly at a known price without significant loss of principal; marketability means being able to sell in an identifiable market. An MMDA is liquid but can only be redeemed with the bank, so it is not marketable.

q: Owen buys a 26-week Treasury bill with a $10,000 face value for $9,880 and holds it to maturity. What is his holding period return, and how is the $120 taxed?
o: 1.20%; ordinary income for federal tax only
1.21%; ordinary income for federal and state tax
1.21%; long-term capital gain for federal tax
1.21%; ordinary income for federal tax only
e: Income = $10,000 − $9,880 = $120. HPR = $120 ÷ $9,880 = 1.21%. The discount is interest: ordinary income for federal purposes, taxed at maturity, and exempt from state and local income tax.

q: Gwen is in a 24% federal and 6% state bracket (ignore any interaction between the two). She earns $500 of discount income on a T-bill and $500 of interest on a bank CD. How much more total income tax does the CD interest cost her than the T-bill income?
e: T-bill: federal only = $500 × 24% = $120. CD: federal and state = $500 × (24% + 6%) = $150. Difference = $150 − $120 = $30, the state tax the T-bill avoids.

q: A government securities dealer sells Treasuries to a money market fund for $4,990,000 and agrees to buy them back in 7 days for $5,000,000. What does the fund earn?
o: Nothing; the fund is the borrower and pays the dealer $10,000
A $10,000 capital gain, because the deal is legally a sale
$10,000 of interest, about 0.20% for the 7 days
$10,000 of interest, about 0.20% per year
e: A repo is essentially a collateralized loan from the buyer to the dealer. Interest = $5,000,000 − $4,990,000 = $10,000. Repo rate = $10,000 ÷ $4,990,000 ≈ 0.20% for the 7-day term.

q: Hal lives in a high-tax state and wants a money market fund whose income escapes both federal and his state's income tax. Which choice fits best?
o: A single-state tax-exempt fund for his state, noting AMT may apply to private activity bonds
A national tax-exempt fund, since all of its income is free of his state's tax
A Treasury-only taxable money market fund, since its income is free of federal tax
A bank money market deposit account, since FDIC-insured interest is tax-exempt
e: Single-state tax-exempt money market funds hold that state's municipal securities, so residents generally avoid both federal and state income tax. Income from any private activity bonds in the fund may be subject to the alternative minimum tax.

q: Why does commercial paper usually yield slightly more than a Treasury bill of similar maturity?
o: Its interest is exempt from state income tax
Its maturities commonly run up to two years
It is secured by the issuer's receivables and inventory
It is slightly less liquid and carries more default risk
e: Commercial paper is an unsecured, negotiable note from a large corporation, maturing in 270 days or less and often backed by bank credit lines. Versus T-bills it is a bit less liquid and riskier, so it pays a modestly higher yield.

q: A small U.S. importer can't get credit from its overseas supplier and is too small to issue commercial paper. Which money market instrument is built for this need?
o: Eurodollar CD
Banker's acceptance
Repurchase agreement
Negotiable CD
e: With a banker's acceptance, the importer's bank pays the foreign supplier and the importer repays the bank, typically within three to six months. The bank may sell the draft at a discount. Firms too small for commercial paper often use them.

q: Priya bought 200 shares of Delta Grid for $11,000. This year she sells all 200 for $8,200, and 18 days later she buys 200 Delta Grid shares for $8,600. What is her basis in the new shares?
e: Loss = $11,000 − $8,200 = $2,800. Buying back within 30 days (2026 edition figure) makes it a wash sale, so the loss is not recognized now. New basis = $8,600 cost + $2,800 disallowed loss = $11,400 ($57 a share).

q: Rina bought 100 more shares of a stock on March 1. On March 21 she sells 100 older shares of the same stock at a $1,500 loss. What is the tax result?
o: A $1,500 loss is allowed because the purchase came before the sale
No loss now, and the $1,500 is permanently lost
No loss now; the $1,500 reduces the basis of the March 1 shares
No loss now; the $1,500 is added to the basis of the March 1 shares
e: A wash sale occurs when similar securities are acquired within 30 days before or after a loss sale (2026 edition figure). The March 1 purchase is 20 days before the sale, so the $1,500 loss is deferred and added to the basis of those shares.

q: Leon has a $9,000 long-term gain, a $4,000 long-term loss, a $2,500 short-term gain and an $11,500 short-term loss this year. What is the result?
o: Deduct the full $4,000 net loss this year
Deduct $3,000 this year and forfeit the other $1,000
Deduct $3,000 this year and carry $1,000 forward
Deduct a $9,000 short-term loss and pay LT rates on $5,000
e: LT: $9,000 − $4,000 = $5,000 gain. ST: $2,500 − $11,500 = $9,000 loss. Cross-net: $5,000 − $9,000 = $4,000 net loss. Deduct $3,000 (2026 edition figure); carry the remaining $1,000 forward indefinitely.

q: Dmitri, a single filer, has MAGI of $230,000, including $45,000 of net investment income. Using the textbook's $200,000 threshold for single filers, what is his net investment income tax?
e: NIIT = 3.8% (2026 edition figure) × lesser of NII ($45,000) or MAGI over threshold ($230,000 − $200,000 = $30,000). Tax = 3.8% × $30,000 = $1,140.

q: Which cash dividend is most likely to qualify for the preferential 0%/15%/20% rates?
o: From a REIT whose shares the client has held for three years
From a C corporation stock held from 45 days before to 45 days after the ex-dividend date
From an S corporation in which the client owns shares
From a C corporation stock bought 10 days before and sold 20 days after the ex-dividend date
e: Qualified dividends come from C corporations (income taxed at the corporate level first) and require holding the stock more than 60 days during the 121-day period that starts 60 days before the ex-dividend date (2026 edition figure). Qualified dividends are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%.

q: Pia sells shares of a gold ETF she held for three years at a gain. What is the maximum federal rate on that long-term gain?
e: Gold and silver ETFs are generally treated as collectibles, and long-term gains on collectibles (art, metals, gems, coins, stamps, antiques) face a maximum 28% rate (2026 edition figure), not the 0/15/20% rates.

q: Jae owns 100 shares with a $30 per-share basis and receives a $2 per-share distribution identified as a return of capital. What is the tax effect?
o: No current tax; his total basis falls to $2,800
$200 taxed as a qualified dividend; basis stays $3,000
$200 taxed as ordinary income; basis falls to $2,800
No current tax; his total basis rises to $3,200
e: A return-of-capital dividend is untaxed because it returns the investor's own money; instead it reduces basis. New basis = ($30 − $2) × 100 = $2,800.

q:
For a client who lives in State X, which statements are correct?
I. Interest on a U.S. Treasury note is federally taxable but exempt from state income tax.
II. Interest on a State X municipal bond is generally exempt from federal and State X income tax.
III. Interest on a State Y municipal bond is exempt from State X income tax.
IV. Interest on a corporate bond is taxable at both the federal and state level.
o: I and III only
II and III only
I, II, III, and IV
I, II, and IV
e: Treasury interest: federal yes, state no. Corporate interest: taxable at both levels. Municipal interest: generally federal-exempt, and state-exempt only for bonds issued in the investor's home state, which can make in-state munis double tax-exempt.
